source.title: Sub-Scaling Laws: On the Role of Data Density and Training Strategies in LLMs
source.authors: Zheng-Yu Chen; Siqi Wang; Teng Xiao; Yudong Wang; Shiqi Chen; Xun-Liang Cai; Junxian He; Jin-Gang Wang

record.file_problem: none noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates loss scaling and compute allocation, reports departures from traditional scaling in high-density and over-training settings, and proposes a modified scaling law.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the study's own loss, performance, allocation, and scaling-fit results. Prior-work results and hyperparameter values used only to configure training are not recorded as rows. Several curve values are figure-only; where the text describes their direction, the state follows that description.
record.test_reason: The authors train over 400 LMs (20M–7B) on Pile variants of different density and over-training ratios. They report where traditional power-law loss fits bend and lose predictive accuracy, and propose a modified Chinchilla-form law. This is an argument that V1, V2 and V7 need restating, backed by the study's own loss and MAPE results.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that high data density and non-optimal model/data allocation (over-training) cause sub-scaling, and that their density- and OTR-aware sub-optimal law predicts better in these regimes. They also state that batch size and learning rate are not causes, and that an optimal OTR of about 20 confirms Chinchilla's allocation.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains models from 20 million to 7 billion parameters on datasets of differing density, examines over-training ratios and fixed-compute allocations, and compares traditional fits with proposed sub-optimal formulations; it is not a direct reproduction of either original study's full method.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with dataset density, OTR, training-token amount, model size, and choice of scaling-law formulation.

fits_no_version.finding: The optimal batch size and learning rate follow power laws in training loss, independent of model size and OTR. Non-optimal hyperparameters hurt from the start of training rather than causing sub-scaling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal batch size and learning rate scale as power laws of the target loss, robust to over-training ratio.

record.problems: The authors state that results rely on specific model architectures and configurations, focus predominantly on over-training, and need further validation with larger models and more training tokens. Many plotted outcomes have no numerical values or uncertainty estimates in the text. The reported experiments are stated to involve over 400 models, but detailed per-model evidence is not supplied for every aggregate claim.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result omitted. Figure-only curves are recorded without estimating plotted values.

untested.parts: Separate power laws in N and D with the other non-bottlenecked are not reported. Most fits are on training loss, not held-out loss.
Extrapolation over orders of magnitude in model size or compute. The Table 4 predictions use the first quarter of a run's own curve plus smaller models.
No fitted exponents for compute-optimal N and D. The Kaplan vs Hoffmann split is addressed only through an OTR of about 20.
Not tested; depth and width co-vary with size in Table 3.
Not tested; text pretraining only, with no controlled repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer experiment.
Only MMLU accuracy on 7B models across checkpoints; no other tasks, and no loss-to-task mapping.
Parameter-counting conventions and training schedule are not varied.

missing.what: Hoffmann-form law predicts loss too optimistically for OTR>750 when fitted on OTR≤750; the Kaplan form predicts too pessimistically (500M model)
The rate of loss improvement per unit compute falls as OTR rises, across model sizes
Fitted modified-law exponents αD=0.289 and αN=0.272, with logistic R factors k1=0.00810 and k2=0.00114
The authors' own performance-scaling test on LLaMA 2 vs LLaMA 3: LLaMA 2 70B outperforms LLaMA 3 8B as FLOPs increase
The minima of fixed-compute loss curves trace the Chinchilla optimal-allocation curve

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The record's V1 links on downstream (MMLU) and curvature rows were moved to V6 and V7. Rows that score the authors' own law were relinked to V7 only. The text claims the sub-optimal law beats the others 'across all model sizes', but Table 4 shows Hoffmann better at 4B and tied at 700M. Table 4 'prediction' extrapolates from the first quarter of training, not across orders of magnitude, so the V2 evidence is short-range. Most loss results are on training loss, and many are figure-only, with no uncertainty beyond the Shapiro-Wilk test.

versions.untested_parts: The paper examines loss scaling in its tested model, data-density, and over-training settings; it does not establish a general law across all language models or a full independent sweep of parameters, tokens, and compute with each of the other quantities non-bottlenecked.
Prediction is evaluated in the paper's tested model sizes and training-token regimes; extrapolation to much larger runs or orders of magnitude beyond these experiments is not established.
The paper studies allocation at fixed compute and discusses an OTR near 20 as optimal, but does not fit separate stable power laws for compute-optimal parameter count and token count.
The experiments concern text language-model pretraining; other modalities, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested. The paper does not report a controlled repeated-data experiment.
Downstream evidence is limited to the reported MMLU accuracy curves; predictability across a broad range of downstream tasks is not tested.
The study compares density and allocation settings and several fit formulations, but does not systematically vary parameter-counting conventions or all possible fitting choices.
